items.item: A feature joined on a table's current state instead of the event's own time lets every future update leak into a training row that predates it.

items.item: Each feature's own freshness need, not a blanket policy, decides whether it runs on batch or on a stream.

items.item: A join on the latest value reaches into the future; the join has to land on what was known at the event's own time.

at.step: Reveal: the point-in-time join, and the leak it closes

items.item: The leaking join's score was optimistic by a measured, specific margin, not a vague risk.
A parity check run once at launch catches nothing later; it has to be a standing SLO with its own alert.

at.step: Reveal: parity as a continuous SLO

items.item: Adding a feature means reconstructing its point-in-time values from raw history, not turning it on only from today.

at.step: Reveal: backfilling a new feature's history

items.item: At ten times the feature count, the next bottleneck is the parity check's own sampling and alert volume, not the join itself.

at.step: Prove it: ten times the features

items.item: This topic leaves out ML modelling, feature engineering and embeddings, the online store and stream engine internals, and model training itself.
One feature definition feeding both stores, point-in-time joins, and continuous parity checks are each established practice, not an emerging technique.
This platform serves software; the next two designs serve a factory floor where sensors lose their network and must keep running.
